paras: The Rushford lynching threat against Jacob Pruchker took place in September 1881 near Rushford, Fillmore County, Minnesota, after a "Bohemian boy" was accused of shooting dead a farmer's daughter, Anna Martin. A search party captured him at his home before dawn and threatened him until he confessed, and threats to lynch him followed while he was held in custody. No harm to him was reported, and the papers treated the case mainly as a murder without motive.

According to a dispatch dated September 15, Anna Martin, daughter of George Martin, a farmer living about three miles from Rushford, was walking home from a neighbor's with her two sisters about 9 p.m. on Tuesday night. As the girls passed a ravine they met a boy with a gun, who fired on them without warning and disappeared "with a yell," and Anna Martin fell dead. The New Ulm Weekly Review instead placed the shooting on "last Wednesday evening."

The district was described as "intensely alarmed and enraged," and parties set out to scour the country for the shooter. From the sisters' "uncertain description," suspicion fell on a Bohemian boy, and about four o'clock in the morning a party went to his home and took him. He at first denied knowing anything, but after being threatened by what one version called "the excited crowd" he confessed, giving no reason.

Once he was in custody, "threats are made to lynch him," the Bismarck Tribune's dispatch said, "but great precautions to prevent have been taken." The St. Paul version warned that the threats "may result in making it warm for him yet," and the New Ulm Weekly Review reported the community "shocked and indignant" amid "some wild talk of lynching."

The boy was arrested and held, and no report of an attack on him appears in the coverage. No report of an inquest, examination or trial was found, and the latest item, in the Mankato Free Press on September 30, said only that a small boy had killed a little girl "just for the fun of the thing."

The story ran in the white press as a wire dispatch, first in the Bismarck Tribune on September 16 and in fuller form in the Watertown Republican of Wisconsin on September 21. That dispatch called the killing "a most horrible tragedy," stressed that the girl was "of a good family and of excellent reputation," and reported the lynching threats without comment. The St. Paul Daily Globe ran it under "Minnesota Murders" as a "brutal murder" and did not mention lynching, nor did a brief in the Batesville Guard of Arkansas, which named the boy "Frank Pruchek."

Papers differed on the boy's name, printing Pruchker, Pruchek, Pruschek and Brucka. They agreed in presenting him as mentally disturbed, calling him "evidently a lunatic" or a "half-witted youth" with a "morbid blood-thirstiness," and none described anyone involved as Black.

reader.title: Rushford lynching threat against Jacob Pruchker
bases: The episode is a threatened lynching: a party seized the accused boy at his home and threatened him into confessing, and threats to lynch him were made while he was in custody, but no violence beyond threats is reported (A1, A3, A4).

No report says the accused was killed or harmed; he was held in custody amid threats to lynch him and 'some wild talk of lynching' (A1, A3, A4). The threats were made in response to the shooting he was accused of (A1).

The Bismarck special dispatch and the St. Paul wire in the Watertown Republican both report the seizure, coerced confession and threats (A1, A4), and the New Ulm Weekly Review separately reports talk of lynching (A3); the shooting and arrest are also in A2 and A5.

accounts.label: Rushford/St. Paul wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A boy fired on the Martin sisters at a ravine and fled with a yell; a party seized the suspected Bohemian boy at home at 4 a.m., he confessed under threats, and threats were made to lynch him in custody.

accounts.label: New Ulm Weekly Review
accounts.gist: A half-witted youth with a 'morbid blood-thirstiness' fired into a group of girls on Wednesday evening; he was arrested amid 'some wild talk of lynching'.

accounts.label: Short briefs
accounts.gist: The St. Paul Daily Globe, Batesville Guard and Mankato Free Press reported the shooting and confession or the bare killing without mentioning lynching threats.

framing.detail: The wire called it 'a most horrible tragedy', stressed the girl's 'good family' and 'excellent reputation', and reported the lynching threats without comment, adding that they 'may result in making it warm for him yet'.
Minnesota papers framed it as a motiveless murder by a disturbed boy ('Minnesota Murders', 'half-witted youth', 'for the fun of the thing') and called the lynching talk 'wild'.

conflicts.note: Spelling varies across reprints of the same wire; no local Rushford paper was found to settle it.
The dispatches dated Sept. 15 say Tuesday night, which is the more contemporary evidence.
